To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) young animals are not consistently more sensitive than adults, to lower doses, for OP and pyrethroids; 2) the greater sensitivity of the neonate, at high doses, is due to limited metabolic capability; 3) ChE inhibition is a sensitive and reliable indicator of OP toxicity and the critical effect in all of our studies; 4) ChE activity is not consistently reduced in neonates exposed to low doses of OP insecticides; and, 5)

(i) the critical effect for OP insecticides is cholinesterase inhibition, (ii) the critical effect is the same in adults and neonates, (iii) neonates are more susceptible than adults to a high dose of Type II pyrethrins but not to lower levels of these compounds or to OP insecticides.
young rats are not more sensitive (i.e., have a lower NOEL) than adults for OP or pyrethyroid insecticides when the exposure is to a low dose.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of age-related differences in susceptibility to insecticides.
understanding the basis for the differences in sensitivity of neonatal and adult animals to OP and pyrethroids.
the question of whether infants and children are more sensitive to low levels of exposure to organophosphates and pyrethroids than are adults.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no age-dependent differences in sensitivity to OP and pyrethroids in the rat at environmentally relevant doses.
young animals are less sensitive than adults at environmentally relevant dose levels of both OP and pyrethroids.
young animals are more sensitive than older animals to a lethal dose of OP or pyretroid insecticides but that they are no more sensitive to lower doses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the greater susceptibility of neonates to OP and pyrethroids is due to a lack of metabolic capacity, and that the greater susceptibility to pyrethroids at lethal doses is due to the kinetics of these compounds.

the greater susceptibility of neonates to OP and pyrethroids at high doses appears to be due primarily to limited metabolic capacity, whereas at lower doses the neonate is not more sensitive than the older animal.

the greater sensitivity of the neonate to acute doses of OP and pyrethroids is not a reflection of an inherent difference in sensitivity of target sites but rather a reflection of limited metabolic capacity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the existing safety factors are sufficient to protect children.
the greater sensitivity of neonates to acute doses of OP and pyrethroids is not relevant to environmental exposures, which are at levels far below that which would cause ChE inhibition.
the existing tolerances provide protection for the young and the old.
